4.0.0.en: 1 "Nebuchadnezzar the king, unto all people, nations, and languages, that dwell in all the earth; Peace be multiplied unto you. 2 I thought it good to shew the signs and wonders that the high God hath wrought toward me. 3 How great are his signs! and how mighty are his wonders! his kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and his dominion is from generation to generation."

4.0.1.en: "Nebuchadnezzar the king, unto all people, nations, and languages, that dwell in all the earth;

4.0.3.en: St. Jerome says that Nebuchadnezzar's letter was recorded among the prophets, so that no one might afterward claim that the book was not Daniel's composition, meaning by this the pagan Porphyry who attacked the book.

4.0.4.en: Nebuchadnezzar presents to us a royal letter issued from the depths of his heart after passing through the divine discipline into which he fell because of his arrogance. He was not ashamed to address this letter to all peoples, nations, and languages that dwell in all the earth, in which he declares the following:

4.0.5.en: a. It was the ancient custom of great kings to count themselves kings over all the earth, although the Babylonian Empire did not reach Gaul and other lands. So it was with Rome during the Roman Empire, which was called the seat of the empire of the whole world, although the empire did not extend to the whole world at that time.

4.0.6.en: b. A testimony from experience of the personal relationship between God and him, for He wrought signs and wonders toward him. Though God humbled him with severe discipline, he deserved this discipline, which was profitable to him. He glorifies God by acknowledging God's care for him, and by acknowledging his sins and that he deserved the discipline.

4.1.0.en: "I thought it good to shew the signs and wonders that the high God hath wrought toward me" [2].

4.2.0.en: c. He bears witness to God's surpassing power: "How great are his signs! and how mighty are his wonders!" [3]. By His signs here he means what St. Jerome says: [By the mercies of God (the king) was restored to his throne, so he praised the King of heaven and glorified Him, on the ground that all His works are truth and His ways judgment, and He is able to abase those who walk in pride].

4.2.1.en: d. He bears witness to the eternal Kingdom of God and His dominion that does not pass away, whereas human kingdoms, however great, must collapse.

4.2.2.en: "His kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and his dominion is from generation to generation" [3].

4.2.3.en: Note that the introduction of the decree carries a theological, biblical, theocratic language (the rule of God), and some see that this reveals Daniel's influence on the king and on his language.

4.2.4.en: God spoke with the king whom He had set as head over all the earth at that time, and yet the king grew in arrogance and pride. He bore witness to God with his mouth, but his heart was haughty. His awareness of the one holy God was temporary, and with his confession of Him he did not withdraw from his worship of pagan gods and his mistaken beliefs.

4.3.s.en: 2. The summoning of the wise men to interpret his dream:

4.3.0.en: "4 I Nebuchadnezzar was at rest in mine house, and flourishing in my palace: 5 I saw a dream which made me afraid, and the thoughts upon my bed and the visions of my head troubled me. 6 Therefore made I a decree to bring in all the wise men of Babylon before me, that they might make known unto me the interpretation of the dream. 7 Then came in the magicians, the astrologers, the Chaldeans, and the soothsayers: and I told the dream before them; but they did not make known unto me the interpretation thereof. 8 But at the last Daniel came in before me, whose name was Belteshazzar, according to the name of my god, and in whom is the spirit of the holy gods: and before him I told the dream, saying,

4.3.1.en: I Nebuchadnezzar was at rest in mine house, and flourishing in my palace" [4].

4.3.2.en: Before Nebuchadnezzar recounts the judgments of God that came upon him because of his pride, he gave a just account of the warning that was directed to him [4], when he was at rest in his house and flourishing in his palace. Recently he had defeated Egypt, and so all his victories over Syria, Phoenicia, Judea, Egypt, and Arabia were completed, and the wars were finished for him in the 34th or 35th year of his reign (Ezek 29:17). These successive victories gave him an opportunity to exercise the haughtiness of his heart and his pride. He felt that there were no longer any clouds in the sky of his life, and that there was no arm able to resist him or stand before him. He thought that peace had come and security was sure.

4.3.3.en: Some translate the word "at rest (selueh)" as "abundance"; for when a man receives in overflowing measure he becomes like the horse which, when it eats more food than necessary, grows unruly, and its rider cannot control it and lead it, and the rider is exposed to falling from it. Therefore God often restrains our bellies and does not give us all that we desire, not because He wants to deprive us, but because He wants us to walk as is fitting for us, so that we do not harm ourselves or Him.

4.3.4.en: "I saw a dream which made me afraid, and the thoughts upon my bed and the visions of my head troubled me.

4.3.5.en: Therefore made I a decree to bring in all the wise men of Babylon before me, that they might make known unto me the interpretation of the dream.

4.4.0.en: Then came in the magicians, the astrologers, the Chaldeans, and the soothsayers: and I told the dream before them; but they did not make known unto me the interpretation thereof" [5-7].

4.4.1.en: Here the king distinguishes this dream from ordinary dreams that spring from his daily circumstances, for he felt that it was an extraordinary dream, carrying a message from the Most High, so he summoned the wise men to interpret the dream.

4.4.2.en: Daniel was in the royal palace, and the king knew him perfectly well, yet he ignored him in order to summon by royal command all the wise men of Babylon before him, the magicians, the astrologers, the Chaldeans, and the soothsayers, setting Daniel apart from them, and when they failed to interpret his dream he resorted to Daniel. He sought the expertise of the magicians while realizing the power and truth of the divine interpretation granted to Daniel the man of God. Had he summoned Daniel it would have been quicker and better for him, but he did not do so. This is often our own conduct, for the prophetic word is in our hands, and divine knowledge is not far from us, and yet we seek human expertise and ignore what is in our hands freely! Let us seek the work of God, who is almighty, all-wise, and loving toward us, who dwells in us, and let us hold fast to His promises, which are not far from us, instead of resorting to what is outside us!

4.4.3.en: The king told the magicians the dream and yet they could not interpret it, they who had said with certainty before: "Let the king tell his servants the dream, and we will shew the interpretation of it" (Dan 2:4, 7). What Isaiah had prophesied before concerning the daughter of Babylon was fulfilled: "Thou art wearied in the multitude of thy counsels. Let now the astrologers, the stargazers, the monthly prognosticators, stand up, and save thee from these things that shall come upon thee" (Isa 47:13).

4.5.0.en: But at the last Daniel came in before me, whose name was Belteshazzar, according to the name of my god, and in whom is the spirit of the holy gods: and before him I told the dream" [8].

4.5.1.en: When all human arms had failed, the king summoned the man of God, Daniel, and told the dream before him. He spoke with him as a pagan king who believes in many gods, but he believes of Daniel that "the spirit of the holy gods is in him" [8].

4.5.2.en: Perhaps the king did not summon Daniel, despite his confidence in his ability to interpret the dream and that no secret is hidden from him, because he realized that the dream carried discipline and humiliation for him to be accomplished by the hands of Daniel's God, so he did not resort to him except under the utmost necessity.

4.6.0.en: "9 O Belteshazzar, master of the magicians, because I know that the spirit of the holy gods is in thee, and no secret troubleth thee, tell me the visions of my dream that I have seen, and the interpretation thereof. 10 Thus were the visions of mine head in my bed; I saw, and behold a tree in the midst of the earth, and the height thereof was great. 11 The tree grew, and was strong, and the height thereof reached unto heaven, and the sight thereof to the end of all the earth: 12 The leaves thereof were fair, and the fruit thereof much, and in it was meat for all: the beasts of the field had shadow under it, and the fowls of the heaven dwelt in the boughs thereof, and all flesh was fed of it. 13 I saw in the visions of my head upon my bed, and, behold, a watcher and an holy one came down from heaven; 14 He cried aloud, and said thus, Hew down the tree, and cut off his branches, shake off his leaves, and scatter his fruit: let the beasts get away from under it, and the fowls from his branches: 15 Nevertheless leave the stump of his roots in the earth, even with a band of iron and brass, in the tender grass of the field; and let it be wet with the dew of heaven, and let his portion be with the beasts in the grass of the earth: 16 Let his heart be changed from man's, and let a beast's heart be given unto him; and let seven times pass over him. 17 This matter is by the decree of the watchers, and the demand by the word of the holy ones: to the intent that the living may know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will, and setteth up over it the basest of men. 18 This dream I king Nebuchadnezzar have seen. Now thou, O Belteshazzar, declare the interpretation thereof, forasmuch as all the wise men of my kingdom are not able to make known unto me the interpretation: but thou art able; for the spirit of the holy gods is in thee."

4.6.1.en: "O Belteshazzar, master of the magicians, because I know that the spirit of the holy gods is in thee, and no secret troubleth thee, tell me the visions of my dream that I have seen, and the interpretation thereof" [9].

4.6.2.en: He called him by the name that he had imposed on him, "Belteshazzar," thinking that by this he was honoring him by ascribing him to his pagan god, whereas the name wounded Daniel's feelings and mind, for on the one hand it deprived him of what his parents had given him as a name connected with the name of the living God, and on the other hand it tied him to an idol in which he did not believe.

4.6.3.en: He also called him "master of the magicians," and this too added to the wounds of his soul, for he wanted to withdraw from the magicians who had deceived the world with their vain sorcery, and did not want to be a chief over them. At the same time he knows two things about him:

4.6.4.en: a. That the spirit of the holy gods is in him [8-9]; what he utters is not from human expertise and temporal wisdom, but from the work of the divine Spirit in him. The king realized that all human expertise and knowledge had failed, so he summoned Daniel, who alone had knowledge springing not from human abilities but from the Spirit of the holy God.

4.6.5.en: b. That no secret is hidden from him [9], which removes from the king his anxiety and the disturbance of his soul.

4.6.6.en: "Thus were the visions of mine head in my bed; I saw, and behold a tree in the midst of the earth, and the height thereof was great.

4.6.7.en: The tree grew, and was strong, and the height thereof reached unto heaven, and the sight thereof to the end of all the earth:

4.6.8.en: The leaves thereof were fair, and the fruit thereof much, and in it was meat for all: the beasts of the field had shadow under it, and the fowls of the heaven dwelt in the boughs thereof, and all flesh was fed of it.

4.6.9.en: I saw in the visions of my head upon my bed, and, behold, a watcher and an holy one came down from heaven; he cried aloud, and said thus,

4.6.10.en: Hew down the tree, and cut off his branches, shake off his leaves, and scatter his fruit: let the beasts get away from under it, and the fowls from his branches:

4.6.11.en: Nevertheless leave the stump of his roots in the earth, even with a band of iron and brass, in the tender grass of the field; and let it be wet with the dew of heaven, and let his portion be with the beasts in the grass of the earth:

4.7.0.en: Let his heart be changed from man's, and let a beast's heart be given unto him; and let seven times pass over him [10-16].

4.7.1.en: Nebuchadnezzar was a lover of the trees of Lebanon; he would go to enjoy them, and bring timber from them for building, so God likened him to the huge tree which he admires.

4.7.2.en: The prophets often refer to the great and the chiefs as trees, as in (Ezek 17:5-7; 31:3, etc.; Jer 22:15; Ps 1:3; 37:35). And the historian Herodotus (Herodotus 7:19) relates that Ahasuerus saw a dream that he was crowned with an olive tree whose branches filled the whole earth, but the crown withered from upon his head, and he realized that his reign would surely end.

4.7.3.en: God wants those in authority and the great, all leaders as well as kingdoms, to be like trees in which all find their nourishment, rest, and security, but men and kingdoms have misused authority, turning it from service into haughtiness with exploitation. For this reason these trees had to be uprooted so that the tree of the Cross might be planted, which brings love and surpassing peace and inward joy to every heart.

4.7.4.en: In this chapter God warns King Nebuchadnezzar, declaring to him in a dream that he will fall under severe discipline because of his arrogance. In this warning we sense God's tenderness in His dealings with man, even with the arrogant pagan king. On the one hand He reveals to him the discipline that will come upon him, that perhaps he might turn back from his evil and be spared it, and He gave him a respite of a whole year to examine himself, but instead of repenting he became haughty. On the other hand, even in the warning He likened him to a useful tree that offers shade to the beasts of the wilderness, food for man and beast, and a dwelling for the birds of heaven, and the tree is also marked by beauty.

4.7.5.en: * Such men are exalted, not by the greatness of their virtues, but by their pride, therefore they are cut down and perish.

4.7.6.en: St. Jerome The king related to Daniel the dream of the huge tree, which was marked by the following:

4.7.7.en: a. Standing in the midst of the earth, growing, and its height reaches to heaven [10-11]. In the midst of the earth, that is, at the center from which the Babylonian imperial authority radiates over all nations and peoples. Both Origen and St. Jerome see that Jerusalem is the center of the earth, as the city of God in which the temple was set up to bless humanity worshipping God. Some Babylonian rabbis (Rabbis) see that Babylon too is in the middle of the earth, as it is on the same line. But from the spiritual side, if Jerusalem represents the heavenly royal palace, then Babylon represents the royal palace of the Antichrist and all his kingdom. If Nebuchadnezzar represents a tree planted in Babylon, the haughty mother of harlots, the true believer represents a tree planted in Jerusalem, in the house of the Lord.

4.8.0.en: b. The sight thereof to the end of all the earth [11].

4.9.0.en: c. Beautiful in appearance [12], a reference to Nebuchadnezzar's concern for architectural constructions and the adorning of the capital.

4.9.1.en: d. Its fruit much, and in it meat for all [12], a reference to the wealth and mighty resources of Nebuchadnezzar.

4.9.2.en: e. A place of protection for others [12], protecting the birds among its branches and the beasts of the field in its shade.

4.9.3.en: This is what God offers to man, to make him a king who dwells in the world like a royal palace, wanting his soul to be always growing. While being on the earth it rises to heaven, that it may rest in the bosom of the Father, be glorified in the ends of the world, beautiful without blemish, satisfying all, widening to embrace others with love and so give security and peace to those who love it!

4.9.4.en: When Nebuchadnezzar fell into pride he deserved discipline, so God sent an angel, whom He called a watcher and an holy one coming down from heaven, to discipline.

4.9.5.en: The angel is called a watcher because he is a spirit without a body, who neither sleeps nor needs rest, so he is ever wakeful night and day. He is also called thus because he moves to carry out God's will for the edification of His people, as the Psalmist says: "Bless the LORD, ye his angels, that excel in strength, that do his commandments, hearkening unto the voice of his word" (Ps 103:20).

4.9.6.en: He is also called holy because he bears no human weakness. We, however, suffer from weakness, not only because of the sins we commit, but because of the corruption that crept into us from our first parents, which afflicts our body as well as our heart and mind.

4.9.7.en: However far a man may attain in sanctification, so long as he is still in the flesh he is not called "the watcher, the holy one," because through the need of nature he must sleep, and through the struggle he is exposed to weaknesses. By this we can distinguish between angels and men, as between striving believers and believers who have put off the body and passed from the world.

4.10.0.en: a. That what happens, even to the pagan king, is not by a human plan but by divine permission. For He sent His watching angel from heaven to carry out this plan. He spoke to him in the language of the Chaldeans, for they believed in heavenly beings who judge the works of men and have authority to decide their fate.

4.11.0.en: b. With the discipline there is mercy, for God commanded that the roots be left in the earth so that the tree might grow again through humility and repentance, so the tree is not uprooted entirely, and the discipline is for a set time, seven times [16]. "For there is hope of a tree, if it be cut down, that it will sprout again, and that the tender branch thereof will not cease. Though the root thereof wax old in the earth, and the stock thereof die in the ground; yet through the scent of water it will bud, and bring forth boughs like a plant" (Job 14:7-9). And though He permitted him to eat grass with the beasts of the field, He did not deprive him of enjoying the dew of heaven.

4.11.1.en: c. The command was given to the beasts that sheltered under the tree and the birds dwelling among its branches to flee, a sign that all the men of the state would forsake him. This is the fruit of sin, that man feels isolation. It is counted that all have forsaken him in moments of distress, even those whose friendship he had won by his lavish gifts.

4.11.2.en: d. It is clear from the dream that the tree symbolizes a particular person, for it personifies the tree, saying in [15-16]: "Let his heart be changed from man's, and let a beast's heart be given unto him"; it did not say of the tree "it" but "he."

4.11.3.en: What does he mean by the heart here? The understanding, the will, the feelings, and the inner soul as a whole. For though trees have no heart, the dream is symbolic. The command issued removed from the king, not only his empire, but also his human nature for a time, for he was not worthy to live as a man even in the lowest degrees of humanity.

4.11.4.en: e. No king arose in his place, but his son Evil-merodach carried out the work during this period until his father returned to his senses and his throne.

4.12.0.en: f. The purpose of the discipline is the benefit of many [17].

4.12.1.en: In this phrase [16] God assures the king that he will not be able to escape the discipline that He declares to him through the dream.

4.12.2.en: "This matter is by the decree of the watchers, and the demand by the word of the holy ones: to the intent that the living may know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will, and setteth up over it the basest of men.

4.12.3.en: This dream I king Nebuchadnezzar have seen.

4.12.4.en: Now thou, O Belteshazzar, declare the interpretation thereof, forasmuch as all the wise men of my kingdom are not able to make known unto me the interpretation:

4.12.5.en: but thou art able; for the spirit of the holy gods is in thee" [17-18].

4.12.6.en: The word "word (pethegma)" here perhaps means a command or decree (edict), as in (Esth 1:20). So what was declared is a divine, heavenly decree. But why is the decree ascribed to the watching holy angels; is it a divine command or an angelic one?

4.12.7.en: Without doubt the command is divine, issued by God alone without any heavenly creature; as for ascribing it here to them, it is to affirm their positive role.

4.12.8.en: With the angels' perfect obedience to God, and their carrying out His commands, they pray for the salvation of the whole world. They ask that God intervene to discipline the proud who blaspheme against God, not to take vengeance on them, but to bring them back to the way of truth. It is as though what issued from God came in harmony with the desire of the heavenly ones' hearts, and their continual petitions, so that the command is counted as though it issued from them.

4.13.0.en: "19 Then Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, was astonied for one hour, and his thoughts troubled him. The king spake, and said, Belteshazzar, let not the dream, or the interpretation thereof, trouble thee. Belteshazzar answered and said, My lord, the dream be to them that hate thee, and the interpretation thereof to thine enemies. 20 The tree that thou sawest, which grew, and was strong, whose height reached unto the heaven, and the sight thereof to all the earth; 21 Whose leaves were fair, and the fruit thereof much, and in it was meat for all; under which the beasts of the field dwelt, and upon whose branches the fowls of the heaven had their habitation: 22 It is thou, O king, that art grown and become strong: for thy greatness is grown, and reacheth unto heaven, and thy dominion to the end of the earth. 23 And whereas the king saw a watcher and an holy one coming down from heaven, and saying, Hew the tree down, and destroy it; yet leave the stump of the roots thereof in the earth, even with a band of iron and brass, in the tender grass of the field; and let it be wet with the dew of heaven, and let his portion be with the beasts of the field, till seven times pass over him; 24 This is the interpretation, O king, and this is the decree of the most High, which is come upon my lord the king: 25 That they shall drive thee from men, and thy dwelling shall be with the beasts of the field, and they shall make thee to eat grass as oxen, and they shall wet thee with the dew of heaven, and seven times shall pass over thee, till thou know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will. 26 And whereas they commanded to leave the stump of the tree roots; thy kingdom shall be sure unto thee, after that thou shalt have known that the heavens do rule. 27 Wherefore, O king, let my counsel be acceptable unto thee, and break off thy sins by righteousness, and thine iniquities by shewing mercy to the poor; if it may be a lengthening of thy tranquillity."

4.13.1.en: "Then Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, was astonied for one hour, and his thoughts troubled him.

4.13.2.en: The king spake, and said, Belteshazzar, let not the dream, or the interpretation thereof, trouble thee.

4.13.3.en: Belteshazzar answered and said, My lord, the dream be to them that hate thee, and the interpretation thereof to thine enemies" [19].

4.13.4.en: We should not wonder at Daniel's bewilderment and his grief over the disaster that was to befall the king of Babylon, for though the king was a tyrant and unjust, who took the Jewish people captive with other peoples, yet since Daniel worked in the palace he was bound to pray for him. God had commanded them by Jeremiah to pray for the prosperity of Babylon, for in this lay their peace (Jer 29:7). And because the seventy years had not yet been completed, it was not right for the believers to ask the king for a return, but they submitted to him in sincere obedience and served him faithfully without hatred. For this Daniel grieved when he learned what would befall the king.

4.14.0.en: "The tree that thou sawest, which grew, and was strong, whose height reached unto the heaven, and the sight thereof to all the earth; whose leaves were fair, and the fruit thereof much, and in it was meat for all; under which the beasts of the field dwelt, and upon whose branches the fowls of the heaven had their habitation: it is thou, O king, that art grown and become strong: for thy greatness is grown, and reacheth unto heaven, and thy dominion to the end of the earth" [20-22].

4.14.1.en: Here Daniel's marvelous wisdom appears, for with his love for the king and his humility before him, and his true longing to rescue him from the disaster, he spoke with him as a servant of the Word with all frankness, and uttered to him the divine truth. The prophet Daniel gives a practical lesson in service, for the servant is gentle with sinners and longs for their salvation, and if he rebukes he does not forget himself as a weak man; and at the same time he does not placate sinners at the expense of the truth, nor conceal God's wrath against sin. The prophet Daniel, who was gentle with the king, did not fear him, but with all boldness said to him: "It is thou, O king." He did not hesitate, nor offer excuses, nor speak in language that shows the slightest doubt, but with certainty declared to him that he is the tree upon which the disaster comes.

4.14.2.en: "And whereas the king saw a watcher and an holy one coming down from heaven, and saying, Hew the tree down, and destroy it; yet leave the stump of the roots thereof in the earth, even with a band of iron and brass, in the tender grass of the field; and let it be wet with the dew of heaven, and let his portion be with the beasts of the field, till seven times pass over him".

4.14.3.en: St. Jerome asks who will bind the king with a band of iron and brass, and answers: [It is very clear; all the insane are bound with chains to keep them from harming themselves or attacking others with weapons].

4.15.0.en: This is the interpretation, O king, and this is the decree of the most High, which is come upon my lord the king" [23-24].

4.15.1.en: While the prophet Daniel affirms that the dream, with all its bitterness, applies to the king, he addresses the king respectfully as "my lord the king." He presents the divine discipline without making light of the king or insulting him with a wounding word.

4.16.0.en: "That they shall drive thee from men, and thy dwelling shall be with the beasts of the field, and they shall make thee to eat grass as oxen, and they shall wet thee with the dew of heaven, and seven times shall pass over thee, till thou know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will" [25].

4.16.1.en: Kings, especially those who are always victorious, often count themselves above every law; they command and are not commanded, they demand the obedience of others and it never crosses their heart to submit to others. They often forget their human nature, as though they were of a nature other than that of all other men. Now the prophet Daniel gives him the interpretation of the dream not to remind him that he is a man with human weakness, but that he will fall under discipline and so lose, together with the kingdom, his human nature, to become on the level of the beasts of the field. He will be cut off from among men to live as among a herd of oxen or swine.

4.17.0.en: "And whereas they commanded to leave the stump of the tree roots; thy kingdom shall be sure unto thee, after that thou shalt have known that the heavens do rule" [26].

4.17.1.en: The prophet Daniel prepares Nebuchadnezzar for repentance, opening to him the door of hope, for with the discipline God's mercies are declared, which await his repentance to restore to him abundantly what he lost. For God disciplines not to humble man, but to lift him up and grant him the gift of knowledge, saying to him "after that thou shalt have known..." So discipline is a divine school for enjoying a surpassing heavenly knowledge.

4.18.0.en: "Wherefore, O king, let my counsel be acceptable unto thee, and break off thy sins by righteousness, and thine iniquities by shewing mercy to the poor; if it may be a lengthening of thy tranquillity" [27].

4.18.1.en: Daniel remained silent for a time, perplexed, so the king felt the gravity of the dream and encouraged him to speak, declaring to him that he would accept the matter whatever it was. Daniel was astonished and his thoughts troubled him for two reasons:

4.18.2.en: a. The fall of a great king like this to the lowest level, that he should have the heart of a beast of the wilderness.

4.18.3.en: b. That it was he who gives the interpretation to the king, and he wished the king well.

4.18.4.en: The king encouraged Daniel to speak, either from a desire to know the truth, or out of curiosity.

4.18.5.en: * He made the truth clear without insulting the king, so as to avoid appearing to accuse the king of sinful pride, but rather of great loftiness.

4.18.6.en: St. Jerome Daniel ended his speech by opening before the king the door of hope through repentance and works of mercy, leaving his sins. Daniel longed for Nebuchadnezzar's repentance so that he would not fall under this severe discipline, but that his enemies would fall into it. Therefore he gave him counsel to be gentle with the poor and needy. By this, as his heart turns from cruelty, violence, and selfishness to love and giving, he finds grace in the eyes of God.

4.18.7.en: * If you open your hands to the poor, Christ also opens His doors to you so that you may enter as into Paradise.

4.18.8.en: Father Caesarius * Let us say that Nebuchadnezzar performed works of mercy with the poor according to Daniel's counsel, therefore the sentence was postponed for twelve months. But when he was walking in his palace in Babylon and said arrogantly: "Is not this great Babylon, that I have built?!"..., he therefore lost the virtue of giving by the evil of his pride.

4.18.9.en: * We also read in Jeremiah of God's instruction to the Jewish people that He obliges them to pray for the Babylonians, for the peace of the captives is bound up with the peace of those who took them captive.

4.19.0.en: "28 All this came upon the king Nebuchadnezzar. 29 At the end of twelve months he walked in the palace of the kingdom of Babylon. 30 The king spake, and said, Is not this great Babylon, that I have built for the house of the kingdom by the might of my power, and for the honour of my majesty? 31 While the word was in the king's mouth, there fell a voice from heaven, saying, O king Nebuchadnezzar, to thee it is spoken; The kingdom is departed from thee. 32 And they shall drive thee from men, and thy dwelling shall be with the beasts of the field: they shall make thee to eat grass as oxen, and seven times shall pass over thee, until thou know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will. 33 The same hour was the thing fulfilled upon Nebuchadnezzar: and he was driven from men, and did eat grass as oxen, and his body was wet with the dew of heaven, till his hairs were grown like eagles' feathers, and his nails like birds' claws. 34 And at the end of the days I Nebuchadnezzar lifted up mine eyes unto heaven, and mine understanding returned unto me, and I blessed the most High, and I praised and honoured him that liveth for ever, whose dominion is an everlasting dominion, and his kingdom is from generation to generation: 35 And all the inhabitants of the earth are reputed as nothing: and he doeth according to his will in the army of heaven, and among the inhabitants of the earth: and none can stay his hand, or say unto him, What doest thou? 36 At the same time my reason returned unto me; and for the glory of my kingdom, mine honour and brightness returned unto me; and my counsellors and my lords sought unto me; and I was established in my kingdom, and excellent majesty was added unto me."

4.19.1.en: "All this came upon the king Nebuchadnezzar.

4.19.2.en: At the end of twelve months he walked in the palace of the kingdom of Babylon.

4.19.4.en: Is not this great Babylon, that I have built for the house of the kingdom by the might of my power, and for the honour of my majesty?

4.19.5.en: While the word was in the king's mouth, there fell a voice from heaven, saying,

4.19.6.en: O king Nebuchadnezzar, to thee it is spoken; The kingdom is departed from thee. And they shall drive thee from men, and thy dwelling shall be with the beasts of the field: they shall make thee to eat grass as oxen, and seven times shall pass over thee, until thou know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will" [28-32].

4.19.7.en: The Hebrew word mehelek indicates that the king was walking on the roof of the palace. The easterners practiced the custom of walking on the roof.

4.19.8.en: The king could see all of Babylon "from the roof," especially if the palace was built on a high hill.

4.19.9.en: In pride he thought he was a god, so he descended to become like a beast, as God said to Job: "behold every one that is proud, and abase him" (Job 10:11). He ascribed everything to himself, his power and his majesty, not to God, the giver of power and wisdom. He also ignored his predecessors who founded the city. But the wise Solomon, who built the temple, says: "Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain" (Ps 127:1).

4.19.10.en: "The same hour was the thing fulfilled upon Nebuchadnezzar: and he was driven from men, and did eat grass as oxen, and his body was wet with the dew of heaven, till his hairs were grown like eagles' feathers, and his nails like birds' claws.

4.20.0.en: And at the end of the days I Nebuchadnezzar lifted up mine eyes unto heaven, and mine understanding returned unto me, and I blessed the most High, and I praised and honoured him that liveth for ever, whose dominion is an everlasting dominion, and his kingdom is from generation to generation" [33-34].

4.20.1.en: In his pride he ascribed to himself Babylon with its walls, its public gardens, its temple of the god Bel, and the royal palace. Herodotus attributes Babylon to Semiramis and Nitocris, while Berosus and Abydenus relate that the Babylonians, that is, Nebuchadnezzar, added much to the old city, for Nebuchadnezzar built a splendid palace and the walls of the city. It may be gathered from Nitocris that Nebuchadnezzar's wife adorned the city.

4.20.2.en: Critics have attacked this text [30], saying that historically Nebuchadnezzar did not build Babylon, but in modern discoveries thousands of bricks were found in Babylon inscribed on the underside "Nebuchadnezzar son of Nabopolassar." Moreover, the word "build" here does not mean mere founding, but is also used for enlarging and adding. And let us not forget that many kings were accustomed to bury the glories of their predecessors and ascribe everything to themselves, by merely changing the form of the thing or adding to it.

4.20.3.en: * Had he not lifted his eyes toward heaven he would not have recovered his former mind.

4.20.4.en: Furthermore, by saying: "mine understanding returned unto me," he showed that he had not lost his outward appearance but only his mind.

4.20.5.en: St. Jerome By saying "from generation to generation" he does not mean only the generations to come, but, as St. Jerome says, that when his mind returned to him he perceived the mystery of the Kingdom of God, which passes from the Law to the Gospel.

4.21.0.en: "And all the inhabitants of the earth are reputed as nothing: and he doeth according to his will in the army of heaven, and among the inhabitants of the earth: and none can stay his hand, or say unto him, What doest thou?" [35].

4.21.1.en: Tyrants often think that God is a prisoner of heaven, with no role in the affairs of men; and they do what they please like gods and there is none to resist them. Now the king sees that the God of heaven moves men, and leads and orders as He wills, and the earth is in the grasp of His hand just as heaven is!

4.22.0.en: At the same time my reason returned unto me; and for the glory of my kingdom, mine honour and brightness returned unto me; and my counsellors and my lords sought unto me; and I was established in my kingdom, and excellent majesty was added unto me [36].

4.22.1.en: Nebuchadnezzar did not repent although God left him twelve months, that is, a whole year after the dream. On the contrary, the king was struck with haughtiness and so the dream was fulfilled in him.

4.22.2.en: The dream was not fulfilled until after a year, God giving the king a long opportunity to examine himself and repent, to be gentle with the captives and care for the needy, but his pride only grew worse.

4.22.3.en: The king was struck with a state of madness that robbed him of his consciousness as a man; he became like the beasts of the wilderness, eating grass. Perhaps he was afflicted with lycanthropy, a disease in which the sufferer imagines that he has been transformed into a wolf.

4.22.4.en: * After that Babylonian king was stripped of the human form in his seven miserable years and became neglected because of his disobedience to the Lord, in bearing the bodily suffering he not only recovered his kingdom, but, what is more, accomplished the good pleasure of God...

4.22.5.en: Tertullian God, who moved Nebuchadnezzar to discipline His people for a time by their captivity, now declares to him that all things proceed with His permission. He permitted his men to drive him from rule and bind him because of his madness, and now He moves them to restore him to the kingship without their perceiving the hidden hand of God.

4.23.0.en: "Now I Nebuchadnezzar praise and extol and honour the King of heaven, all whose works are truth, and his ways judgment: and those that walk in pride he is able to abase" [37].

4.23.1.en: When he completed the period of discipline his mind returned to him, so he lifted his gaze toward heaven as a repentant man seeking the mercies of God. His soul was crushed within him, and he glorified God. He realized that no man can reign forever, and that all kingdoms before God are as nothing. Or perhaps, when Nebuchadnezzar lifted his eyes to heaven glorifying God, God lifted the discipline from him.

4.23.2.en: Some thought that there is no evidence in history pointing to Nebuchadnezzar's madness, which makes the report historically untrue. In Berosus too, as appears in Josephus the Jewish historian, there is something that points to the reality of the king's madness. But it must be pointed out that even if external sources do not contain anything that indicates this madness of the king, this does not mean that the report is historically untrue.

4.23.3.en: "And Daniel continued even unto the first year of king Cyrus" [21].

4.23.4.en: Tame my soul, for it has grown unruly!

4.23.5.en: * You gave me an abundance of good things and gifts, and I was filled and became sated, and my soul grew unruly.

4.23.6.en: Who can tame it but You, who care for my salvation?!

4.23.7.en: * Deprive me of some gifts, grant me humility before You, if there is edification in it for my depths!

4.23.8.en: But do not deprive me of Yourself, for You are the portion of my soul and my eternal inheritance!

4.23.9.en: * I have wronged Your love and the riches of Your gifts, for my soul grew unruly without restraint!

4.23.10.en: How hard it is for me to keep humility of mind amid the abundance of Your gifts!

4.23.11.en: Set my weakness before my eyes, that my mind may be humbled.

4.23.12.en: Take my hand, that I may walk with You in the way of Your love!

4.23.13.en: * Grant me, O Lord, the spirit of Daniel the prophet, the servant.

4.23.14.en: May I long for the salvation of sinners and be gentle with them, yet without flattery at the expense of the divine truth.

4.23.15.en: May I not fear a king however great his tyranny, nor hide Your word however stern it may seem!

4.23.16.en: * Your threats terrified Nebuchadnezzar; I find the sweetness of Your love amid Your threats to me.

4.23.17.en: Teach me to dedicate all my life to obeying You.

4.23.18.en: Your threats and Your promises are for the edification of my soul!

4.23.19.en: * My sin brought me down under divine discipline; it drove me, as it were, into the herd of oxen or swine.

4.23.20.en: Let me return to You, and You will carry me into the fellowship of the saints, and lift me up to the life of the heavenly ones.

4.23.21.en: And grant me a surpassing heavenly knowledge!
